title: ETFDH Alkylation Drives Nitrogen Mustard-Induced Keratinocyte Pyroptosis
authors: Yin Gong; Jia-Yi Ying; Mo Li; An-Ying Wei; Zhi-Peng Pei; Shan-Shan Zhang; Xia-Li Suo; Xiao-Bao Ruan; Xiao-Dan Chong; Ming-Xue Sun; Wen-Qi Meng
abstract: Nitrogen mustard (HN2) is a bifunctional alkylating vesicant that produces blistering and ulcerative skin lesions, yet the molecular events responsible for this tissue damage remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify the direct protein targets of HN2 in human skin and elucidate how target alkylation affects mitochondrial function and thereby causes skin injury. An activity based probe, HNP-1, was designed for fluorescence imaging and chemical proteomic target mapping. Biochemical assays and site-directed mutagenesis were employed to confirm HN2 binding to electron-transferring flavoprotein dehydrogenase (ETFDH) and to identify the modified residue. Additionally, transcriptomic profiling and a murine cutaneous injury model were used to characterize downstream events and evaluate the effects of vitamin B2 (VB2). HNP-1 enabled direct visualization of HN2-derived labeling in skin cells and tissues and showed that the signal was predominantly extranuclear. Unbiased proteomic analysis then identified ETFDH as a high-affinity mitochondrial target. HN2 alkylated ETFDH at His112, impairing its interaction with ubiquinol–cytochrome c reductase core protein 2 (UQCRC2) and triggering mitochondrial oxidative stress, voltage-dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1) oligomerization, and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release. These events promoted cGAS-STING signaling and pyroptosis, whereas the H112A substitution blunted the response. Intraperitoneal VB2 administration restored the epidermal flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) level and attenuated HN2-induced skin injury in mice. These findings link ETFDH alkylation to pyroptotic signaling in acute HN2 skin injury and show that VB2 mitigates skin damage in severely exposed mice.
